# Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway (1938–2024) was a pioneering computer scientist recognized for her transformative contributions to very-large-scale integration (VLSI) chip design. After earning engineering degrees at Columbia University, Conway joined IBM, where she played a key role in the development of superscalar computer architecture. Following her gender transition in 1968, she was dismissed by IBM but later rebuilt her career, joining Xerox PARC in the 1970s. At PARC, Conway co-developed, alongside Carver Mead, the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology and co-authored the influential textbook "Introduction to VLSI Systems." Her scalable design rules and creation of the MOSIS infrastructure revolutionized chip design, democratizing access to fabrication, and overwhelmingly impacted research, education, and the electronics industry. Conway further contributed as an architect of the U.S. Department of Defense's Strategic Computing Initiative at DARPA, and as professor and associate dean at the University of Michigan, specializing in visual communications and hybrid user interfaces. She retired as professor emerita in 1998.
Conway's legacy extends beyond technical innovation—her work fostered the growth of the electronic design automation industry, set the foundry model standard for chip development, and inspired technology startups. Retrospectives, including awards and a 2012 IEEE career special issue, have praised Conway as a major force in VLSI and engineering diversification. She coined the "Conway effect," addressing how innovators from underrepresented groups are often overlooked. A committed transgender rights advocate, Conway shared her transition story widely and championed inclusion and equal opportunity, particularly in STEM fields. Her achievements were recognized with numerous honors, including induction into the Computer History Museum's Fellow Award, the National Academy of Engineering, the National Inventors Hall of Fame, and multiple honorary doctorates. Conway died on June 9, 2024, at age 86.
